title: Stratified GPU commit ladders and enterprise contract Q&A
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Objective: Define a practical, testable set of commit "ladders" (tiered reserved GPU SKUs), burst mechanics, and autoscaling billing primitives that address enterprise procurement patterns and reduce friction in the security questionnaire (SQ) review.

Hypothesis: A stratified commit ladder (Small/Medium/Large pools mapped to predictable throughput ranges) combined with a simple burst credit model and a per-GPU autoscale ramp rate will increase closed-won rate for Dedicated deals by 15% while limiting margin leakage to <8% compared to on-demand pricing. It will also reduce SQ turnaround time by providing prescriptive contract text and standard answers for common security questions.

Scope and deliverables:
- Pricing constructs: definition of three commit ladders (Commit-4, Commit-16, Commit-64) with baseline throughput, guaranteed slots, and a transparent per-minute burst charge.
- Burst behavior: static pool-level burst bucket (credits) and pay-as-you-go overflow with capped nightly cost protections.
- Autoscaling billing: a per-GPU-minute rate for ephemeral autoscale instances plus an optional min-guarantee to avoid cold-start charges.
- SLA tiers: Bronze (99.5%), Silver (99.9%), Gold (99.95%) with mapped response and remediation commitments.
- Contract/SQ pack: template clauses for audit logs, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integration, data segregation, and a pre-filled SQ playbook for standard enterprise questionnaires.
- Acceptance criteria: pricing table + worked examples, 2 customer-facing term sheets, a legal-approved SQ response template, and a pilot with at least two existing accounts on Dedicated.

Key considerations and trade-offs:
- Simplicity vs accuracy: fewer ladders reduce sales confusion but may misprice tail workloads. We opt for three ladders with add-on customization for >Commit-64 customers.
- Burst economics: permissive burst buckets improve UX but increase variable cost. We will model historical tail distributions from 10 pilot customers and set default buckets to contain 95th percentile short-term spikes.
- Autoscale granularity: per-minute billing reduces overcharge risk but complicates metering. We recommend per-minute with 1-minute granularity and minimum 1-minute charge.

Initial pricing mechanics (draft):
- Commit-4: reserved 4 GPUs, baseline rate = $X/hour per GPU (discounted vs on-demand), burst: 40 GPU-min credits per day, overflow rate = 0.9x on-demand.
- Commit-16: reserved 16 GPUs, burst: 200 GPU-min credits per day, overflow rate = 0.85x on-demand.
- Commit-64: reserved 64 GPUs, burst: 1000 GPU-min credits per day, overflow rate = 0.8x on-demand plus negotiation room for annual commits.
- Autoscale spot: ephemeral GPU-minute rate = 0.5x on-demand when capacity available; fallback to overflow rate when not.
- Nightly cap: daily overflow cap = 2x reserved baseline cost to protect customers from runaway bills.

SLA tier mapping (frontline):
- Bronze: 99.5% availability, 8-hour P1 response, best-effort remediation credits.
- Silver: 99.9% availability, 4-hour P1 response, monetary credits up to 10% monthly fee.
- Gold: 99.95% availability, 1-hour P1 response, 25% monthly fee credits and quarterly reliability reviews.

SQ / contract playbook notes:
- Provide pre-approved text for: data residency, network isolation (VPC peering), KMS/HSM options, access controls (RBAC), logging retention windows, and penetration test windows.
- Common SQ Qs pre-seeded: "How is customer data segregated?", "How are keys managed?", "What logging does Redwood provide?", "Do you allow third-party audits?" — each with concise, legal-reviewed answers.
- We will produce an annex with architecture diagrams and operational runbooks to accelerate SOC/SEC vendor reviews.

Pilot and experiment plan:
1) Identify two pilot accounts (one mid-market SaaS, one enterprise) that are already on Dedicated or close to migrating.
2) Offer three-month pilot with suggested ladder and burst settings; instrument at token and GPU-minute level.
3) Run pricing telemetry for 8 weeks; measure margin impact, burst usage distribution, customer satisfaction, and SQ turnaround time.
4) Iterate pricing buckets and contract language, then broad-launch if metrics meet target thresholds.

Success metrics:
- Commercial: 15% increase in Dedicated conversion rate, average contract value uplift of 22%.
- Financial: gross margin on Dedicated >= 60% after burst usage, overflow leakage <8%.
- Op/time: median SQ response time reduced from baseline (current) 18 business days to <=7 business days using the playbook.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: customers game burst buckets -> Mitigation: abuse detection signals + rate-limited enrollment for new customers.
- Risk: underpriced long-tail workloads -> Mitigation: add telemetry guardrails and automatic nudges with usage forecasts.
- Risk: legal pushback on SLA credits -> Mitigation: align with Finance and Legal now; use credit formulas rather than unlimited indemnities.

Next steps:
- Financial modeling (Finance + Prod) — due 2025-02-24.
- Legal review of SQ playbook and SLA wording — kickoff 2025-02-18.
- Select pilot customers and sales enablement materials — 2025-02-28.
